sections.html:
Central Montana's Great Falls is the Cascade County seat and the third largest city in the state: 60,442 people in 22.9 square miles at the 2020 count, inside a county of 84,414. The Missouri River flows through, and dams on three of its falls produce the hydropower behind the Electric City nickname.

No employer matters more to local housing than Malmstrom Air Force Base. The base counts about 3,371 active-duty members, 525 Air Force civilians and some 3,300 family members on or near the property, and put its fiscal year 2025 economic impact near $444 million.

Assignments rotate on a schedule, and a family holding orders may have only a short window to leave. Waiting on a buyer's loan approval can feel painfully slow in that position.

  • With orders in hand, give your report date to every buyer and agent at the outset.
  • Compare how long a cash closing takes against a financed one.
  • Say whether the house is vacant, which can move the closing date.

sections.h2: Freeze, thaw and what weather does to a house
sections.html:
Long, snowy winters, hot dry summers and the occasional chinook wind define the year here, and winter afternoons top 50 degrees about fifteen times over three months. Expect big swings: 20.8 nights at 0 degrees or colder, 44 days that never get above freezing, and about nineteen days reaching 90 degrees.

Freeze and thaw cycles punish foundations and driveways. Roofs deal with snow and summer storms, and furnaces and water heaters work through long heating seasons. Put an aging roof or a shaky furnace in your disclosure, since a buyer's inspector will find it anyway.

sections.h2: Who to call in Great Falls
sections.html:
QuestionOffice and phone
Code complaint on private propertyPlanning and Community Development, 406-455-8574
Code issue in the public right-of-wayPublic Works, 406-771-1401
Property tax bill or paymentCascade County property tax office, 406-454-6850

Complaints drive property code enforcement in Great Falls, and the usual subjects are rubbish, junk vehicles and upkeep. A neighbor's complaint can leave an open case that complicates a sale, so close it out before listing or tell the buyer what is outstanding. Nine neighborhood councils give you a way to hear what is going on near your street.

sections.h2: How Great Falls property taxes are billed
sections.html:
Cascade County sends the bills and collects the money, normally mailing residential bills in late October. Half is due November 30 (or 30 days after the postmark, if later) and half May 31. Homes are revalued every two years at 100 percent of market value. The property tax office is at 121 4th Street North, Suite 1A.

The title company usually settles any unpaid tax for the current period at closing. Request a payoff figure beforehand so the amount is no surprise at signing.

sections.h2: What a seller must tell the buyer
sections.html:
Montana expects a Great Falls seller to disclose in writing any adverse material facts the seller really knows. Section 70-20-502 names title issues, water and wastewater systems, structural and mechanical trouble, additions built without a permit, hazardous materials, drainage and soil problems, and radon, mold or lead-based paint testing.

Deliver it before or alongside the contract; if it arrives later, section 70-20-504 lets the buyer rescind within three days. Section 70-20-503 lists lighter duties for court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales, transfers to a spouse, child or parent, and transfers between co-owners.

sections.h2: Steps for a seller with orders
sections.html:
If a transfer set your move date, work backward from it. Confirm the amount you owe on any mortgage and on property tax. Decide whether you can wait for a financed buyer or need a date you control. Collect the documents a title company will ask for: your latest tax statement, mortgage payoff, and the names of everyone on the deed. Tell any buyer if the house will be empty, because that can move the closing date. After closing, the deed is recorded and the proceeds reach you, so you can leave on your report date with the house handled.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which are the two steps most likely to slip a closing. The trade is price: the offer reflects the repairs and risk the buyer takes on, so compare it in writing before you decide.

Three routes are realistic. Pick based on the house's condition and your deadline.

  • Traditional listing. Most buyers see it, though showings, an inspection and a buyer's loan add time and may bring repair requests.
  • For sale by owner. The agent's commission stays with you, along with the marketing, the negotiating and the disclosure forms.
  • Cash sale to a house-buying company. The buyer accepts the property as is, no loan needs approval, and closing can be timed around your move. The price covers the repairs and risk the buyer absorbs, so measure the written offer against your likely net from a listing.

No cash offer is guaranteed. A buyer has to see the house and the title first.

Walk the property the way a buyer's inspector would. Look at the foundation and driveway for freeze and thaw damage, check the roof after a summer storm, and run the furnace and water heater before the heating season. Clear rubbish, junk vehicles and overgrowth so a code complaint cannot surface mid-sale. Then write down what you know: any repair you made, any problem you have seen and any addition built without a permit. That list becomes your disclosure statement, and a seller who gives it early rarely faces the three-day rescission issue later.

Finally, gather your tax paperwork. Cascade County's property tax office at 406-454-6850 can confirm what has been paid, and the title company will use that number at closing.

sections.h2: Situations that push owners to sell
sections.html:
• A military move with a fixed report date.
  • An older house near the river or downtown with aging wiring, plumbing or a roof near the end of its life.
  • An inherited house shared by several heirs, some out of state.
  • An open code complaint over junk, rubbish or an unmaintained yard.
  • A rental with tenants or deferred repairs that the owner no longer wants to manage.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell a house in Great Falls?
faqs.a: Timing depends on the title, the buyer and how ready you are. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, which are the steps that often slow a financed sale.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix a Great Falls house before selling it for cash?
faqs.a: No. A cash buyer purchases the house as it is. You still must disclose problems you know about under Montana law.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a code complaint on my Great Falls property?
faqs.a: For private property, call Planning and Community Development at 406-455-8574. For the public right-of-way, call Public Works at 406-771-1401.

faqs.q: When are Cascade County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later, and the second half is due May 31. The county property tax office can be reached at 406-454-6850.

faqs.q: Is the Malmstrom workforce a reason Great Falls homes sell quickly?
faqs.a: Malmstrom is the largest employer in the community, and the base reports about 3,300 family members on or near it. How quickly any one house sells still depends on its condition, location and price.
